preamble: In central and eastern Old French the diphthong ei (from Latin tonic ē and ĭ in open syllables) backed and rounded its nucleus to oi in the 12th century; Norman and other western/northern dialects (and Anglo-Norman) kept ei. The oi then developed to [we] and [wa] in later French (roi, moi, toile). The change is essentially confined to French.

examples.note: Archaic rei vs classical roi; northern dialects kept /rei̯/.
Meis survives as the early, northern and Norman form.

sources: Pope, M. K. (1952). From Latin to Modern French with Especial Consideration of Anglo-Norman Phonology and Morphology. Manchester University Press.
Kibler, W. W. (1984). An Introduction to Old French. Modern Language Association of America.
